html:
Río de Oro ("river of gold") was the southern part of the Spanish colony on the Atlantic coast of the Sahara, the later Spanish Sahara. The map shows it on its own from 1914 to 1938.

The name goes back to Portuguese sailors of the 1400s, who took a long bay for a river and hoped it led to the gold of West Africa. There was no river and no gold. Spain claimed the coast in 1884, in the years of the Berlin Conference, and built a small post at Villa Cisneros, now Dakhla.

For decades Spain held little more than that post. The desert inland belonged to Sahrawi nomads who herded camels and moved freely across borders that existed only on paper. Spain joined Río de Oro with Saguia el-Hamra to the north to form Spanish Sahara. Today it is part of disputed Western Sahara.
